Model comparison: Explanation of `model_compare()`

Florence Bockting

2026-11-11

Source: vignettes/articles-online-only/model-comparison.Rmd
model-comparison.Rmd

Introduction

This vignette introduces the loo::model_compare() function. Use model_compare() instead of the deprecated loo::loo_compare() (see the note below).

This vignette shows how to use the function. It does not explain how to interpret the results. It also does not explain what to do in the Bayesian workflow when you get diagnostic warnings, for example high Pareto-k values. For these topics, see the “TODO-case study-model_compare vignette” [Link-TODO].

This vignette does not derive the formulas behind <measure>_diff and <measure>_se_diff (introduced below). For the derivations, see the supplement (TODO-Vehtari et al., 2026).

model_compare() accepts the output of these functions:

  • loo(), kfold(), and waic()
  • <type>_pred_measure(), where <type> is loo, kfold, test, or insample

model_compare() is new in loo v3.0.0. It compares models on several predictive performance measures, for example elpd, mae, rmse, and acc. For the full list, see the Predictive model performance: Overview of measures vignette. You can also define custom measures.

This vignette uses the output of <type>_pred_measure(). It also briefly shows how it compares to the deprecated loo_compare() output. The vignette explains:

  1. The arguments and output of model_compare().
  2. Which standard error model_compare() uses for each built-in measure.
  3. How to compute the difference and its standard error for a custom measure.

Relation between model_compare and loo_compare

The loo_compare function has traditionally been used for model comparison in loo, accepting any object that inherits from the loo class (such as those produced by loo(), kfold(), and waic()).

With the introduction of the pred_measure family, we have deprecated loo_compare and introduced model_compare. While model_compare retains full backward compatibility, it also expands functionality to handle outputs from the pred_measure family.

loo_compare still works and is still a generic, so methods registered by other packages keep dispatching, but it now warns and is frozen at its previous behavior: loo objects compared on ELPD only. The pred_measure sources and custom measures described in this article require model_compare. loo_compare will be removed in a future release. For more details, see vignette("migration-guide", package = "loo").

Running example (count data)

To illustrate the functionality of model_compare() we first introduce a running example. In this example, we compare three Poisson regression models fitted to the roaches data from rstanarm (Gelman and Hill, 2007). This data set records a pest-management trial in 262 apartment buildings. The outcome y is the number of roaches caught in traps after treatment and ranges from 0 to 357. The predictors are:

  • roach1: pre-treatment roach count (used as sqrt_roach1 = sqrt(roach1))
  • treatment: whether the building received pest management
  • senior: whether the building is restricted to elderly residents

The three models used in the following comparison tasks are defined as follows:

  m1:      y ~ treatment + senior
  m2:      y ~ sqrt_roach1 + senior
  m3:      y ~ sqrt_roach1 + treatment

As performance criteria we select six predictive performance measures: elpd, mae, mse, rmse, r2, and rps computed by loo_pred_measure.

Note that rps is the only one of these that needs the posterior predictive draws ypred; the error measures are computed from the posterior expectation mupred (see the input requirements table in ?loo_pred_measure).

Running example

The running example shows how to call model_compare(). It does not show how to interpret the results. For that, see [TODO-LINK]. We therefore do not discuss diagnostic flags or interpretation of the output here.

library(loo)
#> This is loo version 3.0.0
#> - Online documentation and vignettes at mc-stan.org/loo
#> - As of v2.0.0 loo defaults to 1 core but we recommend using as many as possible. Use the 'cores' argument or set options(mc.cores = NUM_CORES) for an entire session.
library(brms)
#> Loading required package: Rcpp
#> Loading 'brms' package (version 2.23.2). Useful instructions
#> can be found by typing help('brms'). A more detailed introduction
#> to the package is available through vignette('brms_overview').
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'brms'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     ar
measures <- c("elpd", "mae", "mse", "rmse", "r2", "rps")

The classical loo_compare output

As the actual model building workflow is not the focus of this tutorial, we fit the three models here without further comment. add_criterion() attaches a loo object (as returned by loo::loo()) to each fit.

SEED <- 42

data(roaches, package = "rstanarm")
roaches$sqrt_roach1 <- sqrt(roaches$roach1)

fit_m1 <- brms::brm(
  y ~ treatment + senior,
  data = roaches,
  family = poisson,
  prior = brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = b),
  chains = 2, iter = 400, seed = SEED, refresh = 0
)
fit_m2 <- update(fit_m1, formula = y ~ sqrt_roach1 + senior,
                 newdata = roaches, refresh = 0)
fit_m3 <- update(fit_m1, formula = y ~ sqrt_roach1 + treatment,
                 newdata = roaches, refresh = 0)

add_loo <- function(fit) {
  brms::add_criterion(fit, criterion = "loo", moment_match = TRUE,
                      save_psis = TRUE)
}
fit_m1 <- add_loo(fit_m1)
fit_m2 <- add_loo(fit_m2)
fit_m3 <- add_loo(fit_m3)

loos <- list(m1 = fit_m1$criteria$loo, m2 = fit_m2$criteria$loo,
             m3 = fit_m3$criteria$loo)

Passing these loo objects to the classical loo_compare() reproduces the familiar ELPD-only comparison, and warns once per session that model_compare() is now the preferred function:

loo_compare(loos)
#> Warning: 'loo_compare' is deprecated. Use 'model_compare' instead.
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff       diag_elpd
#>     m3       0.0     0.0      NA           2 k_psis > 0.62
#>     m2    -211.0   226.1    0.82           2 k_psis > 0.62
#>     m1   -2752.6   637.6    1.00           8 k_psis > 0.62
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.

When we use model_compare instead, we get the same output for loo objects:

model_compare(loos)
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff       diag_elpd
#>     m3       0.0     0.0      NA           2 k_psis > 0.62
#>     m2    -211.0   226.1    0.82           2 k_psis > 0.62
#>     m1   -2752.6   637.6    1.00           8 k_psis > 0.62
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.

It also supports the simplify argument in the print method:

print(model_compare(loos), simplify = FALSE)
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff       diag_elpd elpd_loo se_elpd_loo
#>     m3       0.0     0.0      NA           2 k_psis > 0.62  -5465.3       669.8
#>     m2    -211.0   226.1    0.82           2 k_psis > 0.62  -5676.3       772.3
#>     m1   -2752.6   637.6    1.00           8 k_psis > 0.62  -8218.0       876.3
#>  p_loo se_p_loo   looic se_looic
#>  216.4     55.4 10930.7   1339.5
#>  181.1     41.8 11352.6   1544.5
#>  271.1     56.4 16436.0   1752.6
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.

Basic usage

We now use loo_pred_measure() to compute the predictive performance for each model (m1, m2, m3) and measure (see list above). Finally, we compare the performance of the three models using model_compare(). By default, only the ranking measure is shown. The ranking measure is elpd when all models share it. Otherwise, it is the first shared measure in alphabetical order.

fit_measure <- function(fit, measure) {
  loo_pred_measure(
    loo = fit$criteria$loo,
    y = fit$data$y,
    ypred = brms::posterior_predict(fit),
    mupred = brms::posterior_epred(fit),
    measures = measure
  )
}

set.seed(SEED)
m1 <- fit_measure(fit_m1, measures)
#> Warning: The `loo` object was corrected with "moment_match".
#> ! Only "elpd", "mlpd" and "ic" include this correction.
#> ℹ "mae", "mse", "rmse", "r2", and "rps" use the uncorrected PSIS weights.
m2 <- fit_measure(fit_m2, measures)
#> Warning: The `loo` object was corrected with "moment_match".
#> ! Only "elpd", "mlpd" and "ic" include this correction.
#> ℹ "mae", "mse", "rmse", "r2", and "rps" use the uncorrected PSIS weights.
m3 <- fit_measure(fit_m3, measures)
#> Warning: The `loo` object was corrected with "moment_match".
#> ! Only "elpd", "mlpd" and "ic" include this correction.
#> ℹ "mae", "mse", "rmse", "r2", and "rps" use the uncorrected PSIS weights.

(comp <- model_compare(list(m1 = m1, m2 = m2, m3 = m3)))
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m3, ...).
#> PSIS-LOO unreliable for all 3 models (k_psis > 0.62); measures may be biased.
#>  model bad_k
#>     m1     8
#>     m3     2
#>     m2     2
#> 
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff
#>     m3       0.0     0.0      NA          
#>     m2    -211.0   226.1    0.82          
#>     m1   -2752.6   637.6    1.00
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.
#> 
#> Use print(x, measures = "all") to see all measures.

When we want to see a specific measure, we can change this by passing the information to the print method:

print(comp, measures = "r2")
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m3, ...).
#> PSIS-LOO unreliable for all 3 models (k_psis > 0.62); measures may be biased.
#>  model bad_k
#>     m1     8
#>     m3     2
#>     m2     2
#> 
#> -- r2 (vs m2) --
#>  model r2_diff r2_se_diff
#>     m2   0.000      0.000
#>     m3  -0.005      0.071
#>     m1  -0.219      0.092

If you want to see all columns related to a measure specified in measures use simplify = FALSE:

print(comp, measures = "r2", simplify = FALSE)
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m3, ...).
#> PSIS-LOO unreliable for all 3 models (k_psis > 0.62); measures may be biased.
#>  model bad_k
#>     m1     8
#>     m3     2
#>     m2     2
#> 
#> -- r2 (vs m2) --
#>  model r2_diff r2_se_diff    r2 se_r2
#>     m2   0.000      0.000 0.249 0.094
#>     m3  -0.005      0.071 0.243 0.131
#>     m1  -0.219      0.092 0.030 0.024

If you want to see all measures use measures = "all":

print(comp, measures = "all")
#> Printing 6 measure comparisons; consider `measures = c(...)`.
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m3, ...).
#> PSIS-LOO unreliable for all 3 models (k_psis > 0.62); measures may be biased.
#>  model bad_k
#>     m1     8
#>     m3     2
#>     m2     2
#> 
#> -- elpd (vs m3) --
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff
#>     m3       0.0     0.0      NA          
#>     m2    -211.0   226.1    0.82          
#>     m1   -2752.6   637.6    1.00          
#> 
#> -- mae (vs m3, sign flipped) --
#>  model mae_diff mae_se_diff
#>     m3     0.00        0.00
#>     m2    -0.12        0.70
#>     m1    -7.71        1.67
#> 
#> -- mse (vs m2, sign flipped) --
#>  model mse_diff mse_se_diff
#>     m2      0.0         0.0
#>     m3    -13.5       180.6
#>     m1   -563.4       289.6
#> 
#> -- r2 (vs m2) --
#>  model r2_diff r2_se_diff
#>     m2   0.000      0.000
#>     m3  -0.005      0.071
#>     m1  -0.219      0.092
#> 
#> -- rmse (vs m2, sign flipped) --
#>  model rmse_diff rmse_se_diff
#>     m2       0.0          0.0
#>     m3      -0.2          2.0
#>     m1      -6.0          2.9
#> 
#> -- rps (vs m3, sign flipped) --
#>  model rps_diff rps_se_diff
#>     m3     0.00        0.00
#>     m2    -0.12        0.69
#>     m1    -7.34        1.65
#> 
#> All differences: 0 = best model, negative = worse.
#> Signs flipped for loss measures: mae, mse, rmse, rps.
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.

Output of model_compare()

Using print(., measures = "all") returns a subsection for each measure. The rows represent the different models, with the best model always in the first row, followed by the second best, and so on. The columns:

  • model: Name of each model
  • <measure>_diff: The point estimate representing the difference in the measure between the current model and the reference model (calculated as model - reference). For the reference model itself, this value is always zero.
  • <measure>_se_diff\(^{(1)}\): The standard error of the difference
  • p_worse: (only for elpd) Estimated probability that a model has worse predictive performance than the reference model
  • diag_diff: (only for elpd) Diagnostic column flagging miscalibration of the normal approximation behind p_worse and se_diff

Above the measure subsections, print() names the reference model each set of differences was computed against, and, for loo_pred_measure() inputs, reports the PSIS-LOO diagnostic once per model:

  • bad_k: Number of observations whose Pareto \(\hat{k}\) exceeds the PSIS reliability threshold. Pareto \(\hat{k}\) describes a model’s PSIS-LOO approximation.

This block is omitted when no model is flagged, and for kfold, test, and insample sources, which have no Pareto \(\hat{k}\) diagnostic.

\(^{(1)}\) The only measure that deviates from this naming convention is elpd, where the column is called se_diff instead of elpd_se_diff for backwards compatibility.

The measure_info attribute

Each model has a measure_info attribute, which provides meta information for each performance measure.

meta <- attr(m1, "measure_info")

# measure info for each single measure (e.g., R2)
names(meta$r2)
#> [1] "loss"        "diff_method" "se_diff_fun" "extra"

The information is stored in different slots:

slot description functionality
loss Whether the measure is a loss (TRUE; lower values of the measure are better) or a utility (FALSE, higher values are better) During model comparison, loss measures have their sign flipped so that all differences are reported on a utility scale (higher is better)
diff_method How paired pointwise differences are aggregated within model comparison: "sum", "mean", "measure_specific", or "custom" Selects the formula for <measure>_se_diff (see the table in Section Computation of the standard error)
se_diff_fun Name of the measure’s own standard-error function for computing <measure>_se_diff, only set when diff_method = "measure_specific" ("rmse", "r2", "bacc") Points to the built-in function that computes <measure>_se_diff for measures whose estimate is not a plain sum or mean of pointwise values
extra Optional auxiliary data the measure stored for its se_diff_fun, on the measure’s natural scale (e.g., mse_y_i for r2, class_id for bacc); NULL for measures that need none Carries the quantities the standard error needs but the pointwise values do not contain; passed to se_diff_fun() as part of each model’s input

How model_compare() computes the output

This section relates <measure>_diff and <measure>_se_diff to the model objects. All measures use the same point estimate. The standard error depends on the measure. For the formulas, see the supplement (TODO-Vehtari et al., 2026, Section TODO-ARXIV-SECTION).

Computation of the point estimate <measure>_diff

The estimates elpd_diff, mae_diff, rmse_diff, and r2_diff in the output of the running example represent the point estimates of the pairwise model comparisons. They are computed as the measure-specific difference between two model estimates (comparison model - reference model).

For example, the difference in elpd between model m1 (comparison) and model m3 (reference) is computed as follows:

m1_elpd <- m1$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"]
m3_elpd <- m3$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"]

m1_elpd - m3_elpd

This computation is done for each measure and each pairwise model comparison.

By default, however, the reference model is chosen per measure as the best model for that measure. The reference used for each measure is recorded in the compare_reference attribute:

models <- list(m1 = m1, m2 = m2, m3 = m3)
ref <- attr(comp, "compare_reference")
ref
#> elpd  mae  mse   r2 rmse  rps 
#> "m3" "m3" "m2" "m2" "m2" "m3"

The following code block shows, for model m1, the hand-computed differences against each measure’s own reference model and the differences reported in the comp object:

est <- function(x, measure) x$estimates[measure, "Estimate"]
measures_all <- c("elpd", "mse", "mae", "rmse", "r2")

data.frame(
  reference = ref[measures_all],
  by_hand   = sapply(measures_all, function(m) {
    est(m1, paste0(m, "_loo")) - est(models[[ref[[m]]]], paste0(m, "_loo"))
  }),
  reported  = sapply(measures_all, function(m) {
    comp[[paste0(m, "_diff")]][comp$model == "m1"]
  })
)
#>      reference       by_hand      reported
#> elpd        m3 -2752.6484331 -2752.6484331
#> mse         m2   563.4409737  -563.4409737
#> mae         m3     7.7100076    -7.7100076
#> rmse        m2     5.9957668    -5.9957668
#> r2          m2    -0.2187693    -0.2187693

Note that in the above output, the sign for some measures is flipped between the by_hand and reported column, specifically for mse, mae, and rmse. These measures are losses (see callout box below).

However, when we compare all measures together, we want them all to be on the same scale, which in our case is the utility scale. Therefore, losses are converted to the utility scale. As such, higher values are always better. Consequently, the best model has the highest value, and when the best model is also the reference model, the estimated difference <measure>_diff (computed as comp - reference) is always non-positive.

When a measure is converted to the utility scale, print() marks it with “sign flipped” in the table header. It also names it below the tables:

comp <- model_compare(list(m1 = m1, m2 = m2, m3 = m3))
print(comp, measures = c("r2", "mae"))
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m3, ...).
#> PSIS-LOO unreliable for all 3 models (k_psis > 0.62); measures may be biased.
#>  model bad_k
#>     m1     8
#>     m3     2
#>     m2     2
#> 
#> -- r2 (vs m2) --
#>  model r2_diff r2_se_diff
#>     m2   0.000      0.000
#>     m3  -0.005      0.071
#>     m1  -0.219      0.092
#> 
#> -- mae (vs m3, sign flipped) --
#>  model mae_diff mae_se_diff
#>     m3     0.00        0.00
#>     m2    -0.12        0.70
#>     m1    -7.71        1.67
#> 
#> All differences: 0 = best model, negative = worse.
#> Signs flipped for loss measures: mae.

Utility vs. loss scale

We call a measure a loss when it has, by default, the orientation lower is better.

By contrast, we call a measure a utility if it has, by default, the orientation higher is better.

Which orientation a measure has can be inspected from the loss slot of the measure_info attribute of the model object:

sapply(meta, function(x) x$loss)
#>  elpd   mae   mse  rmse    r2   rps 
#> FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

Computation of the standard error <measure>_se_diff

The standard error summarizes the uncertainty in the estimated difference. Depending on the measure, different approaches for computing the standard error are used. We summarize them in four different categories:

diff_method SE of the difference Measures Supplement
"sum" sqrt(N) * sd(d_i) elpd, ic Eq. TODO-ARXIV
"mean" sd(d_i) / sqrt(N) mlpd, mae, mse, acc, brier, rps, srps Eq. TODO-ARXIV
"measure_specific" the measure’s own se_diff_fun rmse, r2, bacc Eq. TODO-ARXIV
"custom" declared via custom_measure(se_diff_fun = ) custom measures –

where N is the number of observations and d_i the paired difference of the pointwise estimates of the two models (comparison - reference).

The user can check which approach is used for each measure via the diff_method slot in the measure_info attribute of the model object:

sapply(meta, function(x) x$diff_method)
#>               elpd                mae                mse               rmse 
#>              "sum"             "mean"             "mean" "measure_specific" 
#>                 r2                rps 
#> "measure_specific"             "mean"

Custom measures

A custom measure is any function returning a list with estimate, se, and pointwise. Define it with custom_measure(), which attaches three declarations to the function:

argument of custom_measure() attribute meaning
name measure_name the name under which the measure is reported
loss measure_loss TRUE if lower values are better (default FALSE)
se_diff_fun measure_se_diff how model_compare() computes the SE of a difference

A custom measure always gets diff_method = "custom". Setting the attributes directly with attr() gives the same result.

The argument se_diff_fun accepts one of three things:

value meaning
"mean" estimate is the mean of the pointwise values. SE is computed as sd(d_i) / sqrt(N)
"sum" estimate is the sum of the pointwise values. SE is computed as sqrt(N) * sd(d_i)
a function custom function for computing the SE, called as fn(ref, cmp)

With se_diff_fun = NULL (the default), the measure declares nothing. model_compare() then reports the difference with an NA standard error and a message. model_compare() needs no further argument in either case.

We elaborate on these points in the following examples.

Example (one custom measure)

In the following, we provide a custom measure that is not part of the built-in measures. The Huber loss is quadratic for small residuals and linear for large residuals. We define it as follows:

huber_fn <- function(y, mupred) {
  delta <- 10
  r <- y - colMeans(mupred)
  l <- ifelse(abs(r) <= delta, 0.5 * r^2, delta * (abs(r) - 0.5 * delta))
  list(estimate = mean(l), se = sd(l) / sqrt(length(l)), pointwise = l)
}
huber_se_fn <- function(ref, cmp) {
  d <- cmp$pointwise - ref$pointwise
  sd(d) / sqrt(length(d))
}

huber_measure <- custom_measure(
  fun = huber_fn,
  name = "huber",
  se_diff_fun = huber_se_fn,
  loss = TRUE
)

With name, we report the measure as “huber”. With loss = TRUE, we declare that it is a loss rather than a utility (i.e., lower values are better). Note that a custom measure is by default considered to be a utility. The argument se_diff_fun declares the standard error of the difference. It is called as huber_se_fn(ref, cmp), where each argument is a list describing one model with elements estimate, se, pointwise, and extra. This is the general form. The shorthands "mean" and "sum" cover the two common cases.

A custom measure is by default considered to be a utility (i.e., higher values are better).

This can be changed with custom_measure(loss = TRUE) (see example above).

First, we compute the predictive performance measures for two different models using "rmse" and the custom Huber loss as performance criteria.

h1 <- fit_measure(fit_m1, measure = list("rmse", huber_measure))
#> Warning: The `loo` object was corrected with "moment_match".
#> ! Only "elpd", "mlpd" and "ic" include this correction.
#> ℹ "rmse" and "huber" use the uncorrected PSIS weights.
h3 <- fit_measure(fit_m3, measure = list("rmse", huber_measure))
#> Warning: The `loo` object was corrected with "moment_match".
#> ! Only "elpd", "mlpd" and "ic" include this correction.
#> ℹ "rmse" and "huber" use the uncorrected PSIS weights.

(Remember that we have created the fit_measure helper at the beginning of this tutorial. It simply wraps loo_pred_measure().)

Inspecting the attribute measure_info shows that the Huber loss uses diff_method = "custom", and that our declaration is recorded as se_diff_fun.

str(attr(h1, "measure_info"))
#> List of 3
#>  $ elpd :List of 3
#>   ..$ loss       : logi FALSE
#>   ..$ diff_method: chr "sum"
#>   ..$ se_diff_fun: NULL
#>  $ rmse :List of 3
#>   ..$ loss       : logi TRUE
#>   ..$ diff_method: chr "measure_specific"
#>   ..$ se_diff_fun: chr "rmse"
#>  $ huber:List of 3
#>   ..$ loss       : logi TRUE
#>   ..$ diff_method: chr "custom"
#>   ..$ se_diff_fun:function (ref, cmp)

model_compare() reads the declaration from the objects, so the comparison needs no further argument:

comp_h <- model_compare(list(m3 = h3, m1 = h1))
print(comp_h, measures = "huber")
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (huber: m3, rmse: m3).
#> PSIS-LOO unreliable for both models (k_psis > 0.62); measures may be biased.
#>  model bad_k
#>     m1     8
#>     m3     2
#> 
#> -- huber (vs m3, sign flipped) --
#>  model huber_diff huber_se_diff
#>     m3        0.0           0.0
#>     m1      -75.0          16.2
#> 
#> All differences: 0 = best model, negative = worse.
#> Signs flipped for loss measures: huber.

As discussed above, the difference estimates are always reported on the utility scale. Therefore huber_diff for m1 is negative.

Extended example (multiple custom measures)

In the following, we extend the example above by adding one further custom measure and show how this is implemented. As an additional custom measure we use RMSE normalized by the standard deviation of the outcome:

nrmse_fn <- function(y, mupred) {
  sqe <- (y - colMeans(mupred))^2
  list(
    estimate = sqrt(mean(sqe)) / sd(y),
    se = sqrt(var(sqe) / length(sqe)) / (2 * sqrt(mean(sqe))) / sd(y),
    pointwise = sqe,
    extra = list(sd_y = sd(y))
  )
}

nrmse_se_fn <- function(ref, cmp) {
  n <- length(ref$pointwise)
  mse_ref <- mean(ref$pointwise)
  mse_cmp <- mean(cmp$pointwise)
  se_ref <- sqrt(var(ref$pointwise) / n)
  se_cmp <- sqrt(var(cmp$pointwise) / n)
  cov_rc <- sum((cmp$pointwise - mse_cmp) * (ref$pointwise - mse_ref)) /
    (n * (n - 1))

  rel_ref <- se_ref / sqrt(mse_ref)
  rel_cmp <- se_cmp / sqrt(mse_cmp)
  rho <- cov_rc / (se_ref * se_cmp)

  # the RMSE formula of the supplement (Eq. TODO-ARXIV), written so
  # that a model compared against itself cancels to exactly zero
  se_rmse <- 0.5 * sqrt(
    (rel_cmp - rel_ref)^2 + 2 * rel_cmp * rel_ref * max(1 - rho, 0)
  )

  se_rmse / ref$extra$sd_y
}

nrmse_measure <- custom_measure(
  fun = nrmse_fn,
  name = "nrmse",
  se_diff_fun = nrmse_se_fn,
  loss = TRUE
)

Subsequently, we compute the predictive performance measures for two different models using "rmse", the custom Huber loss, and the custom normalized RMSE ("nrmse") as performance criteria.

n1 <- fit_measure(fit_m1, list("rmse", huber_measure, nrmse_measure))
#> Warning: The `loo` object was corrected with "moment_match".
#> ! Only "elpd", "mlpd" and "ic" include this correction.
#> ℹ "rmse", "huber", and "nrmse" use the uncorrected PSIS weights.
n3 <- fit_measure(fit_m3, list("rmse", huber_measure, nrmse_measure))
#> Warning: The `loo` object was corrected with "moment_match".
#> ! Only "elpd", "mlpd" and "ic" include this correction.
#> ℹ "rmse", "huber", and "nrmse" use the uncorrected PSIS weights.

Finally, we perform model comparison with multiple custom measures. Both measures declare their own se_diff_fun, so no argument is needed:

comp_n <- model_compare(list(m3 = n3, m1 = n1))
print(comp_n, measures = "all")
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (huber: m3, nrmse: m3, rmse:
#> m3).
#> PSIS-LOO unreliable for both models (k_psis > 0.62); measures may be biased.
#>  model bad_k
#>     m1     8
#>     m3     2
#> 
#> -- huber (vs m3, sign flipped) --
#>  model huber_diff huber_se_diff
#>     m3        0.0           0.0
#>     m1      -75.0          16.2
#> 
#> -- nrmse (vs m3, sign flipped) --
#>  model nrmse_diff nrmse_se_diff
#>     m3      0.000         0.000
#>     m1     -0.124         0.075
#> 
#> -- rmse (vs m3, sign flipped) --
#>  model rmse_diff rmse_se_diff
#>     m3       0.0          0.0
#>     m1      -5.8          4.0
#> 
#> All differences: 0 = best model, negative = worse.
#> Signs flipped for loss measures: huber, nrmse, rmse.

Comparing other predictive sources

model_compare() treats every *_pred_measure() result the same way. Only the constructor changes. All models in one call must share one source. A mixed call is an error.

K-fold cross-validation

brms::kfold() refits each model K times, so this is the most expensive step in this article.

set.seed(SEED)
folds <- kfold_split_random(K = 5, N = nrow(roaches))

kfold_measure <- function(fit, measure) {
  kf <- brms::kfold(fit, folds = folds, save_fits = TRUE)

  kfold_pred_measure(
    y = fit$data$y,
    ypred = brms::kfold_predict(kf, method = "predict")$yrep,
    mupred = brms::kfold_predict(kf, method = "fitted")$yrep,
    kfold = kf,
    measures = measure
  )
}

k1 <- kfold_measure(fit_m1, measures)
#> Warning: Found 21 observations with a pareto_k > 0.61568910657988 in model
#> 'fit'.
k2 <- kfold_measure(fit_m2, measures)
#> Warning: Found 13 observations with a pareto_k > 0.61568910657988 in model
#> 'fit'.
k3 <- kfold_measure(fit_m3, measures)
#> Warning: Found 21 observations with a pareto_k > 0.61568910657988 in model
#> 'fit'.

model_compare(list(m1 = k1, m2 = k2, m3 = k3))
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m3, ...).
#> Predictive measures evaluated on 5-fold cross-validation.
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff
#>     m3       0.0     0.0      NA          
#>     m2    -273.7   222.1    0.89          
#>     m1   -2847.8   610.6    1.00

print() names the source above the table. The PSIS-LOO block is gone, because Pareto \(\hat{k}\) describes the LOO approximation only.

Held-out test data

Here we hold out 60 buildings, refit each model on the rest, and score the held-out ones. ylp_test supplies elpd_test; ylp stays the training log-likelihood.

set.seed(SEED)
test_id <- sample(nrow(roaches), 60)
roaches_train <- roaches[-test_id, ]
roaches_test <- roaches[test_id, ]

test_measure <- function(fit, measure) {
  fit_train <- update(fit, newdata = roaches_train, refresh = 0)
  test_pred_measure(
    y = roaches_test$y,
    ypred = brms::posterior_predict(fit_train, newdata = roaches_test),
    mupred = brms::posterior_epred(fit_train, newdata = roaches_test),
    ylp = brms::log_lik(fit_train),
    ylp_test = brms::log_lik(fit_train, newdata = roaches_test),
    measures = measure
  )
}

t1 <- test_measure(fit_m1, measures)
#> Start sampling
t2 <- test_measure(fit_m2, measures)
#> Start sampling
#> Warning: Bulk Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior means and medians may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bulk-ess
#> Warning: Tail Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior variances and tail quantiles may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#tail-ess
t3 <- test_measure(fit_m3, measures)
#> Start sampling
#> Warning: Bulk Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior means and medians may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bulk-ess
#> Warning: Tail Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior variances and tail quantiles may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#tail-ess

model_compare(list(m1 = t1, m2 = t2, m3 = t3))
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m2, ...).
#> Predictive measures evaluated on held-out test data (N = 60).
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff
#>     m2       0.0     0.0      NA          
#>     m3     -46.1    55.1    0.80   N < 100
#>     m1    -666.2   212.0    1.00   N < 100
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.
#> 
#> Use print(x, measures = "all") to see all measures.

In-sample

In-sample scores need no refit. They are optimistically biased and favor the more complex model, so model_compare() warns:

insample_measure <- function(fit, measure) {
  insample_pred_measure(
    y = fit$data$y,
    ypred = brms::posterior_predict(fit),
    mupred = brms::posterior_epred(fit),
    ylp = brms::log_lik(fit),
    measures = measure
  )
}

i1 <- insample_measure(fit_m1, measures)
i2 <- insample_measure(fit_m2, measures)
i3 <- insample_measure(fit_m3, measures)

model_compare(list(m1 = i1, m2 = i2, m3 = i3))
#> Warning: Comparing in-sample predictive measures. In-sample scores are
#> optimistically biased and favor more complex models. For out-of-sample
#> comparison use loo_pred_measure(), kfold_pred_measure(), or
#> test_pred_measure().
#> Each measure compared against its own best model (elpd: m3, ...).
#> Predictive measures evaluated on in-sample (training) data.
#>  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff
#>     m3       0.0     0.0      NA          
#>     m2    -246.3   210.0    0.88          
#>     m1   -2698.0   610.3    1.00
#> Use print(x, measures = "all") to see all measures.

Everything else in this article, custom measures, the print arguments measures and simplify, works unchanged for all four sources.

Summary

Measure diff_method Standard error
elpd, ic sum sqrt(N) * sd(d_i)
mlpd, mae, mse, acc, brier, rps, srps mean sd(d_i) / sqrt(N)
rmse measure_specific delta method on the MSE scale
r2 measure_specific delta method, including baseline uncertainty
bacc measure_specific stratified by class, paired within class
custom custom from se_diff_fun: your function, “sum”, “mean”, or NA

The things worth remembering:

  1. The difference is always estimate_cmp - estimate_ref, reported so that negative means worse.
  2. The standard error is always paired, because the models are evaluated on the same observations.
  3. NA in a standard error column means “not available”, not “zero” and not “an error occurred”.
  4. A custom measure is assumed to be a utility. If yours is a loss, say so with custom_measure(loss = TRUE), or its differences and its ranking will come out reversed.
